question: Under the Inland Navigation Rules, what horizontal arc must a masthead light cover?
choice_b: 112.5 degrees, visible to one side only
choice_d: 225 degrees -- from right ahead to 22.5 degrees abaft the beam on either side
explanation: A masthead light must show an unbroken light over an arc of 225 degrees, fixed to show from right ahead to 22.5 degrees abaft the beam on either side of the vessel.

question: What horizontal arc does each sidelight (red or green) cover under the Inland Navigation Rules?
choice_a: 112.5 degrees -- from right ahead to 22.5 degrees abaft the beam on its respective side
choice_b: 225 degrees, covering both the bow and the stern
choice_c: 360 degrees, visible all around the vessel
explanation: Each sidelight covers an arc of 112.5 degrees, from right ahead to 22.5 degrees abaft the beam on its own side, so together the two sidelights cover 225 degrees across the bow.

question: What horizontal arc must a sternlight cover under the Inland Navigation Rules?
choice_b: 135 degrees -- 67.5 degrees on each side of dead astern
explanation: A sternlight covers an arc of 135 degrees, fixed to show 67.5 degrees from right aft on each side of the vessel.

question: What is a towing light, as defined under the Inland Navigation Rules?
choice_a: A blue flashing light used exclusively by personal watercraft
choice_b: A green light identical to a starboard sidelight
choice_c: A yellow light with the same 135-degree arc and characteristics as a sternlight, displayed by a vessel that is towing
choice_d: A light not defined anywhere in the Inland Navigation Rules
explanation: A towing light is a yellow light having the same characteristics as a sternlight (135-degree arc, 67.5 degrees each side of dead astern), used by a vessel engaged in towing.

question: For a power-driven vessel 50 meters (about 164 feet) or more in length, what is the minimum visibility distance required for its masthead light?
explanation: On vessels 50 meters or more in length, the masthead light must be visible from at least 6 nautical miles.

question: For a vessel 50 meters (about 164 feet) or more in length, what is the minimum visibility distance required for its sidelights and sternlight?
choice_d: Visibility distance is not specified for large vessels
explanation: On vessels 50 meters or more in length, sidelights and the sternlight must each be visible from at least 3 nautical miles.

question: For a power-driven vessel at least 12 meters (39.4 feet) but less than 50 meters long, what is the required minimum visibility of its masthead light?
choice_a: 6 nautical miles no matter the exact length in that range
choice_b: 5 nautical miles, or 3 nautical miles if the vessel is less than 20 meters (65.6 feet) long
explanation: For vessels 12 meters up to 50 meters long, the masthead light must be visible from 5 nautical miles, except that a vessel under 20 meters need only meet 3 nautical miles.

question: Under the Inland Navigation Rules, which vessels are required to carry a whistle for sound signaling?
choice_a: Only vessels 100 meters or more in length
choice_b: No vessel is required to carry a whistle
choice_c: Vessels 12 meters (39.4 feet) or more in length
explanation: A vessel 12 meters or more in length must be provided with a whistle meeting the technical specifications in Annex III to the Inland Rules.

question: Under the Inland Navigation Rules, what additional sound-signaling equipment must a vessel 20 meters (65.6 feet) or more in length carry?
choice_a: Only a bell, with no whistle required
choice_b: No additional equipment beyond what a 12-meter vessel needs
choice_c: A foghorn instead of a bell
choice_d: A bell, in addition to a whistle
explanation: A vessel 20 meters or more in length must carry a bell in addition to a whistle, with both meeting the technical specifications in Annex III.

question: Under the Inland Navigation Rules, what extra sound-signaling equipment must a vessel 100 meters (about 328 feet) or more in length carry?
choice_a: A gong producing a tone that cannot be confused with the bell
choice_c: A bell alone is sufficient, no gong required
choice_d: No requirement beyond what a 20-meter vessel needs
explanation: A vessel 100 meters or more in length must additionally carry a gong, the tone of which cannot be confused with that of the required bell.

question: Under the Inland Navigation Rules, what sound-signaling equipment must a vessel under 12 meters (39.4 feet) in length carry?
choice_a: It is completely exempt from any sound-signaling requirement
choice_b: It is not required to carry a whistle or bell, but must be provided with some other means of making an efficient sound signal
choice_c: It must carry a full ship's bell regardless of its size
choice_d: It must carry a gong instead of a whistle
explanation: A vessel under 12 meters is not obligated to carry the whistle and bell required of larger vessels, but must have some other means of making an efficient sound signal.

question: Under the Inland Navigation Rules, what lights must a sailing vessel underway display at night, aside from a stern light?
choice_d: No lights are required on a sailing vessel under sail
explanation: A sailing vessel underway must exhibit sidelights and a sternlight, but -- unlike a power-driven vessel -- it does not show a masthead light while under sail alone.

question: For a sailing vessel less than 20 meters (65.6 feet) in length, what lighting option does Rule 25 allow?
choice_a: It must show three separate lanterns mounted at the bow
choice_b: Combined lanterns are prohibited on any sailing vessel regardless of length
choice_c: Only vessels over 65.6 feet may use a combined lantern
choice_d: The sidelights and sternlight may be combined into one lantern carried at or near the top of the mast where it can best be seen
explanation: Rule 25 allows a sailing vessel under 20 meters to combine its sidelights and sternlight into a single tricolor-style lantern near the masthead.

question: What optional additional lights may a sailing vessel show near the top of its mast under Rule 25?
choice_a: Two all-round lights in a vertical line, red above green, but not shown at the same time as a combined lantern
choice_b: Two all-round white lights, required in addition to the combined lantern
choice_d: Green above red, mandatory on every sailboat
explanation: A sailing vessel may optionally exhibit two all-round lights in a vertical line near the masthead, red above green, but these may not be shown together with the combined lantern option.

question: Under Rule 25, what must a vessel under oars or a sailing vessel less than 7 meters (about 23 feet) do at night if it cannot practicably show the normally prescribed lights?
choice_a: It is completely exempt from showing any light under any circumstance
choice_b: Have ready at hand an electric torch or lighted lantern showing a white light, exhibited in time to prevent collision
choice_c: It must still show full sidelights and a masthead light regardless of size
choice_d: It may show a red flare in place of any white light
explanation: If it is not practicable for a vessel under oars or a sailing vessel less than 7 meters to show the prescribed lights, it must have ready at hand an electric torch or lighted lantern showing a white light, shown in time to prevent collision.

question: Under Washington law, during what hours is towing a water skier behind a boat prohibited?
choice_a: Water skiing is allowed at any hour if the tow boat shows an all-round white light
choice_b: There is no time-of-day restriction on water skiing in Washington
choice_c: From one hour after sunset until one hour before sunrise
explanation: Washington law prohibits towing a person on water skis or a similar device from one hour after sunset until one hour before sunrise.
